parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French auvans, from Old French anvant (1180), from Gaulish *andebanno (“eaves, portico”) (compare Occitan ambans, Catalan envà), compound of ande (“intensive prefix”) (compare Welsh an-) + banno (“horn”) (compare Welsh ban), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *an- + *bandā.

parole.significato: chaff (inedible casing of a grain seed)
parole.testo: From Gaulish *balu.
Inherited from Middle French baume, baulme, from Gaulish *balma
From Old French bied, bié, from Gaulish *bedom, from Proto-Celtic *bedom (“something that is dug”), ultimately from the root Proto-Indo-European *bʰedʰ-.
Ultimately from Gaulish *bunda, feminine form of *bundos (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰ-, *bʰudʰmḗn. Cognate with Piedmontese bondon.
Borrowed from Gaulish *bawā.
From a proposed Gaulish *borwa (“hot springs”), related to Gaulish Borvo (“Celtic god of hot springs”).
From Gaulish or Ancient Ligurian. Cognate with Piedmontese busa, Ligurian bêusa, bûsa, bûsia and Occitan bosa, bosia.

From Old French bracier, from brace (“malt”), from Gaulish *brakis (Latinized accusative bracem in Pliny) (compare Scottish Gaelic braich, Welsh brag), from Proto-Celtic *mrakis, from Proto-Indo-European *merk- (“to be soaked”) (compare Latin marceō (“to wither, droop”), North Frisian marig (“tallow
Named after Brie, France, from Gaulish *briga (“hill”). Doublet of Bourgogne.

Unknown origin; possibly of Gaulish origin (compare Catalan bri, Spanish brenca (“fiber”), brinza (“blade of grass, filament”)), from Proto-Celtic *brinikā, from *brinos (“filament, fiber”) (compare Breton broenenn, Welsh brwynen), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrugh-no- (“twig”), perhaps related to th
Borrowed from Gaulish *drudos (“strong, vigorous”).

Borrowed from Gaulish *gobbos, from Proto-Celtic *gobbos (“muzzle, snout, beak”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵoph₃o- (“eat, masticate (of animals)”). Compare Irish gob, Scottish Gaelic gob (“beak, bill”) and English gob.

parole.significato: crawl, a stake enclosure at a body of water to catch fish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Gaulish *gorton ‘hedge, enclosure’; cf. Irish gort, Cornish gorth, Welsh garth.

parole.significato: fallow; fallow land (especially when left uncultivated on purpose)
parole.testo: First attested in 1690. Formerly ‘tillage, land prepared for plowing’, from Old French gaschiere, gaskiere, from Gaulish *gansco (“branch”) (compare Old Irish gesca); from Proto-Indo-European *kak-. Akin to Spanish and Portuguese gancho (“hook”).
Probably of pre-Roman origin, perhaps from Gaulish *lotta, which would explain the preserved -t in French. Of obscure ultimate origin, with no known Celtic cognates of the Gaulish word.
Inherited from Old French marne, variant of marle, from Gaulish *margila, a diminutive of marga, attested in Pliny.
From Gaulish *sagna, compare Latin stāgnum.
Unknown. Possibly from Gaulish *talutum (“slope”), derived from *talu (“front”), from Proto-Celtic *talu (“front”). Compare Latin talutium (“slope containing gold deposits”).
Borrowed from Gaulish trugna (“nose, snout”), which could be related to *srogna (“nose”), from Proto-Celtic *srognā. Cognate with Welsh trwyn, Cornish tron, Breton stroen.
Borrowed from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *wesnālā. Cognate with Old Irish fannall (Irish fáinleog, Scottish Gaelic ainleag) and Welsh gwennol.
